phonemes.desc: Palatal [dʒ] as in 'jump', then short open [ɐ] — the world (jagat) beginning in motion.
Voiced [ɡ] plus a geminate [nː] — the nasal doubled where jagat meets nātha, 'world' joining 'lord'.
The long ā [naː] that carries the name's weight — the lordship, held and sustained.
Aspirated dental [t̪ʰ], a soft 'tuh' with breath — not the English 'th' of 'this'.

pronunciation.approximation: JUH-gun-NAH-thuh — hold the long aa on 'nah', keep the rhythm trochaic, and let the final th be a soft, breathy 'tuh'.

kin.label: Sanskrit
kin.form: jagat, 'the moving world, all that exists' + nātha, 'lord, protector' — Jagannātha, 'Lord of the World'

kin.label: Devanagari
kin.form: जगन्नाथ — IAST Jagannātha; the English word 'juggernaut' descends from this name through colonial-era travellers' accounts

kin.label: Related epithets
kin.form: Puruṣottama, 'the Supreme Person', the Lord's title at Puri; Lokanātha, 'Lord of the World', also a Buddhist epithet

pronunciation.note: Jagannātha is Tier 1 because the Sanskrit form preserves what ASCII flattens: the long ā of -nātha and the geminate n are load-bearing in the IAST restoration, and the name's division jagat + nātha ('Lord of the World') is visible only when the vowel length is written. The earlier placeholder note's claim about 'stress' was wrong — Sanskrit does not mark stress; length and the doubled nasal do the work.

domains.title: Lord of the World
domains.subtitle: Lord of the World, Puri, Devotion
domains.lead: Jagannātha is Viṣṇu as the Lord of the World, worshipped at Puri in Odisha in a form older than any scripture about him: a great-eyed wooden god with no arms, who rides out once a year on a towered chariot pulled by human hands. His mythology is the story of how the world came to Puri — a tribal deity, a king's vow, a carpenter who vanished, and a journey that never stopped.

cards.name: Puruṣottama-kṣetra
cards.desc: Puri, the sacred field where the Lord owns the land itself — in 1238 CE King Anangabhima III dedicated his entire kingdom to him.

cards.name: The Unfinished Hands
cards.desc: The icons have no arms and no legs: the carpenter of the gods vanished before finishing them, and the tradition kept them unfinished on purpose.

cards.name: The Three Siblings
cards.desc: Jagannātha with Balabhadra and Subhadrā on one platform — Kṛṣṇa, his brother, and his sister, worshipped as one household.

cards.name: The Ratha Yātrā
cards.desc: Once a year the Lord leaves the temple and rides a city-high wooden chariot pulled by thousands of hands down the Grand Road to his aunt's house.

symbols.name: The armless form
symbols.meaning: Sovereignty that receives rather than grasps — the Lord needs no hands, because his people's hands are his

symbols.name: The dāru-brahman, the log of Brahman
symbols.meaning: The Lord came to Puri not as an idol but as fragrant timber floating from the sea

symbols.name: The chariot rope
symbols.meaning: To pull it is to be pulled — grace transmitted through the shoulder, not the eye

symbols.name: The Nīlācala, Blue Mountain
symbols.meaning: The hill of Puri the Lord chose as his seat, where the Sabara chief first kept him in secret

symbols.name: Mahāprasāda
symbols.meaning: The sacred food from the world's largest kitchen, eaten by all together without distinction of caste

symbols.name: The round eyes
symbols.meaning: The wide unblinking gaze of the unfinished icons — the Lord watching the world without eyelids

mythology.lead: Jagannātha's mythology is a foundation epic told in temple chronicles and Purāṇic chapters rather than in any single scripture. It tells how the Lord of the World came to the Odia coast: hidden among tribal worshippers, sought by a king, carved by a carpenter who vanished, and carried in person through his own city once every year.

myths.title: The Blue Lord of the Sabaras
myths.text: King Indradyumna of Malwa heard whispers of a wonder: on the remote Blue Mountain of the eastern coast, the tribal chief Viśvavāsu worshipped in secret a form of Viṣṇu called Nīlamādhava, the Blue Lord. The king sent his priest Vidyāpati to find him. Vidyāpati lived among the Sabaras, won the chief's trust, and married his daughter Lalitā; when he was led at last to the hidden shrine, he scattered mustard seed along the path so the king could follow. But a storm swept down and carried the Blue Lord away before Indradyumna arrived. The king fasted on the shore, performed the horse sacrifice at Puruṣottama-kṣetra, and waited. In a dream the god spoke: build a temple, and I will come to you as a log from the sea. The Puruṣottama-khaṇḍa of the Skanda Purāṇa tells the tale, and the temple chronicle Mādala Pāñjī keeps it. The myth absorbs without erasing: the Sabara chief's line holds to this day the hereditary right to touch the god before anyone else.

myths.title: The Carpenter Who Never Finished
myths.text: One dawn a great log of fragrant reddish wood drifted in from the sea — dāru-brahman, Brahman come as timber, bearing the marks of conch, discus, mace, and lotus. An old carpenter arrived unasked and promised the king three images in twenty-one days, on one condition: no one might open the workshop door. Day by day the king waited; on the fourteenth day — the nineteenth in some tellings — the door was opened, and the carpenter was gone. On the platform stood three figures with huge round eyes and no arms: Jagannātha, his brother Balabhadra, his sister Subhadrā. Indradyumna was stricken, but the sage Nārada consoled him: the Lord had chosen the form his people would love, and the unfinished state was no accident but an invitation. The Mādala Pāñjī preserves the story; the Skanda Purāṇa tells a shorter form. A god who cannot hold anything must be held by his people — which is exactly what happens to him every single year.

myths.title: The Journey to Gundicha's House
myths.text: Each summer, in the bright half of the month Āṣāḍha, the three images leave the great temple. Servants carry them swaying down the Bada Dānda, the Grand Road, and set them on three towered wooden chariots — Nandighoṣa for Jagannātha, some twenty metres tall with sixteen wheels — rebuilt from raw timber every year by hereditary carpenters. Hundreds of thousands pull the ropes, and the Gajapati, the king of Puri, sweeps the chariot platform with a golden broom, performing the duty of the humblest sweeper in his own kingdom. For nine days the Lord stays at the Gundicha temple, the house of his aunt Gundicha, and then the whole road walks him home. The temple chronicles record the festival across the centuries, and seventeenth- and eighteenth-century European travellers gave English a new word for an unstoppable mass — juggernaut. Once a year the Lord of the World, who has no feet, travels farther than any god who does.

myths.title: Whose God Is the Lord of Puri?
myths.text: The oldest question about Jagannātha is whose god he is, and the sources disagree by design. The Purāṇic tradition makes him Puruṣottama, Viṣṇu-Kṛṣṇa himself; the founding myth gives him a tribal cradle, the Sabara people of the Blue Mountain. Nineteenth- and twentieth-century scholarship added a Buddhist candidate: K. C. Panigrahi and others argued that the great mound of Puri had once been a stupa, the Buddha's tooth relic its treasure, and the Jagannātha cult a Brahmanical conversion of a Buddhist shrine. The landmark study of Eschmann, Kulke, and Tripathi (1978) refused to choose, reading the god as a layered negotiation — tribal deity, royal legitimation under the Eastern Ganga kings, and finally full Vaiṣṇava identity sealed when Jayadeva's Gītagovinda made Puri a center of Kṛṣṇa devotion in the twelfth century. The debate never closed because it cannot: Puri's god was assembled from all his claimants, and each layer still worships him. A god built by negotiation belongs to everyone who negotiated.

lore.syncretism: Jagannātha is syncretism made architecture. The tribal layer survives in the Sabaras' hereditary service; the Buddhist hypothesis — stupa, tooth relic, converted shrine — hung over the temple through two centuries of scholarship before the Eschmann–Kulke–Tripathi study (1978) reframed the god as a deliberate layering rather than a conversion. Jain memory claims the early mathas of Puri; the Brahmanical settlement made him Puruṣottama, and the devotional revolution of the Gītagovinda made him Kṛṣṇa. Colonial travellers turned his chariot into an English common noun — juggernaut — and the crown of his modern reception belongs to ISKCON: since 1967–68, Prabhupāda's disciples have staged the Ratha Yātrā in San Francisco, London, and every major city on earth, so that the armless god of one Odia town now rides annually through most of the world's capitals. In Puri itself the Gajapati king still sweeps the chariot floor with a golden broom — a living kingship rite older than every republic around it.
lore.culturalLegacy: Jagannātha anchors one of Hinduism's four great pilgrimages — the Char Dham — and Puri's kitchen is the largest in the world, feeding upward of a hundred thousand people a day with mahāprasāda eaten without caste distinction, a daily sacrament of equality run on firewood and hereditary cooks. Every twelve to nineteen years the wooden gods are ceremonially buried and replaced with new neem logs in the rite of Nabakalebara, 'new embodiment' — perhaps the only major cult in which the deity's body is periodically allowed to die. For Odisha, Jagannātha is more than a god: royal inscriptions from 1238 declare him the owner of the kingdom, and modern Odia identity still speaks of the land as his household. And through ISKCON's global Ratha Yātrās and the word juggernaut, the Lord of the World has become, accidentally and thoroughly, a citizen of every city on earth.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Jagannātha is the god who cannot do anything for himself — cannot walk, cannot hold, cannot see without the huge painted eyes — and is therefore the most thoroughly loved god in India. His incompleteness is the theology: a finished god would be finished with us. The carpenter vanished so that the people could take over, and every year they do, rebuilding the chariots, hauling the ropes, sweeping the platform with a golden broom in the king's hands. Sovereignty, in Puri, is redefined as the right to be carried.

To name a domain Jagannātha is to claim that the world's lordship is exercised through other people's hands. The institution that understands this stops polishing its own image and starts building chariots — heavy, wooden, temporary, pulled by strangers. The god returns to his temple each year, but only because the road remembers him. Devotion, the temple says, is not what the god has; it is what the god is missing.

lore.archaeology: The present great temple was begun by the Eastern Ganga king Anantavarman Chodaganga Deva (r. 1078–1150 CE) and completed under his successors, above all Anangabhima III (r. 1211–1238 CE), whose inscriptions of 1238 declare the kingdom itself the property of Puruṣottama-Jagannātha — a rare case of a state legally deeding itself to its god. The Nīlācala hill beneath the temple held older, humbler shrines remembered in the Purāṇic chapters, and the Skanda Purāṇa's Puruṣottama-kṣetra mahātmya claims sanctity far older than any surviving masonry. The images themselves are perishable by design: neem wood, repainted and repaired on a fixed cycle and wholly replaced at the Nabakalebara rite, so the god's body is a documented sequence of bodies. The chariot-yard, the Grand Road, and the Gundicha temple complete a ritual city-plan without parallel — a town whose main street exists so that its god can leave home once a year.
